Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Leo was nineteen when he finally told someone the whole story, sitting in a quiet office with his hands pressed flat against his thighs. Two years earlier, he had been a healthy seventeen-year-old who worked part-time as a peer counselor at a community youth center—a role he took seriously, because listening to other people’s problems gave his own life structure. Then came the fever that would not break, the headache that felt like his skull was splitting, and the emergency room visit that turned into a week in intensive care. Bacterial meningitis, the doctors said. They used words like “sepsis” and “multi-organ failure,” and for three days his family was told to prepare for the worst. He survived, but the memory of those days was not a story he could tell; it was a series of snapshots he could not control. The sharp cold of the lumbar puncture needle. The antiseptic smell that clung to the plastic walls of his isolation room. The sight of the IV line snaking into his own forearm, and the way his body had trembled uncontrollably even when the fever broke.

In the months after discharge, Leo tried to go back to normal. He returned to his counseling shifts, he saw his girlfriend Maria regularly, and he told himself the worst was over. But the triggers began to surface in ways he could not predict. A client mentioned that their grandmother was in the hospital, and Leo felt his throat close. He walked past a first-aid kit in the staff break room and his heart started hammering. He started steering clear of the clinic down the street from the youth center, taking a longer route even when he was running late. His girlfriend suggested they watch a medical drama, and he snapped at her without meaning to. What frightened him most was the way his own body seemed to betray him—a sudden movement from a colleague would make him flinch as if under attack, and his heart would pound for no reason he could name. He began to believe that his body was no longer something he could trust, that it was an enemy that kept sending danger signals even when he knew, logically, that he was safe. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. He went to work because he had to, came home because he had nowhere else to go, and spent the evenings sitting in the dark.

Sleep became a battleground. Leo dreaded the moment his head hit the pillow, because his mind would replay the hospital room, or his body would jolt with a startle response to a car horn outside. He began staying up until two or three in the morning, scrolling through videos on his phone until his eyes burned, just to avoid the moment when he would have to be still with his own reactions. The sleep deprivation made him irritable at work, and more than once a teenager in his counseling group asked if he was okay. He deflected. He avoided thinking about anything that came up in the sessions he had briefly attended after his discharge—a few weeks with a therapist who wanted him to talk about the illness—because the moment he let the memory in, his hands would sweat and his chest would tighten. Better to keep it locked away.

By the time he finally reached out for help, the consequences had become impossible to ignore. He had missed three routine physical exams in a row. He had stopped driving past the hospital, even though it meant taking a twenty-minute detour to the grocery store. Maria had tried to talk to him about a minor infection she had, and he had left the room without a word. She told him, gently but firmly, that she could not watch him disappear like this. Leo sat in the therapist’s office and described his symptoms only when asked directly: the startle responses, the sleeplessness, the way his body kept acting as if it were still in that hospital bed. He did not say it out loud, but deep down he was terrified that if he started thinking about the illness, the story he had buried would swallow him whole. What he wanted, more than anything, was to trust his body again—and he had no idea how to begin.
